The Phase-5 report is done and gated — `PHASE5_FINAL_REPORT.md` (368 lines, 19 sections, repo root), verified against shipped CSVs with 0 forbidden-claim strings. Summary:

**Scope:** 2 cases × 5 locations (F1–F5) × 4 fault types on frozen Phase-4 production data. Outputs in `results/phase5_protection/` (9 CSVs + manifest + sha256 + run log + 2 TCC plots).

**Headline results (all CSV-verbatim):**
| Item | Result |
|---|---|
| Study pickups | GEN-51 15023.75 A, GEN-51N 5 A, GSUT-HV-51 1380 A, GIS-Q0-51 1043.95 A |
| F3 LLL vs 50 kA ref | 50.53 kA, +1.06% — NOTE only, never a verdict |
| F1 LG earth chain | 7.272 A → 0.4848 mA secondary, margin 1.454, t ≈ 1.86 s |
| Coordination (96 rows) | FAIL=20, NO-TRIP=28, NO-PAIR=24, NOT-DET=24, PASS=0 — honest, untuned |
| Breaker duty (41 rows) | 40× NOT DETERMINABLE (no Q0 rating) + 1 NOTE |
| Sensitivity (60 rows) | 16k≡15k×15/16 to 8.9e-16, fenced |
| Validation / suite / gate | 16/16, 355/0, 17/17 |

**Key limitations (§16):** 52-1 bay-position assumption; GEN-51 blind to ~8.4 kA unbalanced branches; 2.27 A thin EF margin; no duty verdict without a Q0 rating; study CTs/TMS/curves assumed. Phase-6 handoff items in §19.

Full A–M deliverable ledger: `.superpowers/sdd/phase5/task-20-deliverable.md`. Reproduce via `run_phase5_production('production')` / `run_phase5_tests()` / `phase5_gate()`.

Want anything beyond this — e.g. the report exported to PDF/DOCX, a shortened executive brief, or the TCC plots pulled into a slide-style summary?

I went through the Phase-5 report, the EEE 305 Protection/Substation slides, and cross-checked the protection architecture against the actual Ashuganj protection/measurement SLD and Siemens generator protection-setting report already in the project source set.

The important conclusion is:

Phase 5 is computationally disciplined, but it is not yet a faithful representation of the physical Ashuganj South protection system.

It is much more accurately described as a generic backup overcurrent/earth-fault coordination study built on the Phase-4 fault currents.

That distinction matters a lot. The report itself correctly says all relay values are study settings rather than commissioned values, and reports 344/0 tests and 16/16 validation legs.

1. The biggest problem: the physical protection scheme is much richer than Phase 5

The actual Ashuganj protection SLD shows a number of functions that Phase 5 does not model:

Generator: 87G, 46, 40, 32R, 21, 78, 59, 81, 24, 64G/59N, 50/27, 50BF, 51/51N and associated trips/lockouts.

GSUT/UAT/GAT: differential and transformer protection functions including 87/87N, 63, 49, 50/51, 50G, 50BF, 59N and 86-related tripping.

230-kV GIS: busbar differential, breaker failure and bay overcurrent functions.

230-kV transmission line: two Siemens 7SD5221 line-protection channels are documented, while the 230-kV busbar protection is Siemens 7SS523.

But Phase 5 has only seven registry entries, dominated by:

GEN-51 → GEN-51N → GSUT-HV-51 → GIS-Q0-51

with line 21 and remote boundary left as notes.

So the current implementation does not model the actual primary protection system.

That is not automatically wrong for an academic project, but the report's title and presentation should not imply that the whole physical protection system has been implemented.

2. GEN-51 is the clearest technical error

This is the most important numerical/protection correction.

Phase 5 currently uses:

pickup = 15,023.75 A
IEC Standard Inverse
TMS = 0.1
resulting F1 LLL operating time ≈ 0.532 s

Those are explicitly the Phase-5 study settings.

But the actual Siemens generator protection report says something materially different.

For the actual 7UM622 generator relay:

50/51 I> is ON.
Inverse overcurrent protection is disabled.
I> pickup is 1.14 A secondary.
That corresponds to approximately 17,171 A primary.
Time delay is 3.00 s, although the Siemens document marks this timing with ??, meaning it requires confirmation/customer coordination information.

The same Siemens report explicitly says the generator overcurrent is a backup stage, and that its final time/curve has to be coordinated with the neighbouring-system grading plan rather than simply assigning a generic inverse curve.

Therefore:

The current Phase-5 GEN-51 calculation is not a physical reproduction of the plant generator 51 protection.

It is a new hypothetical inverse-time backup relay.

That distinction is enormous because:

$$ I_{\text{pickup, Phase5}}=15023.75 A $$

versus

$$ I_{\text{pickup, Siemens}} \approx17171 A $$

and, more importantly,

Phase 5: inverse, ≈0.53 s at F1 LLL
Siemens design report: definite-time I> around 3 s, with timing requiring coordination information.

So the present TCC for GEN-51 is not the plant relay characteristic. It is a study characteristic.

Correction

Create two clearly separated layers:

A. Source-backed generator protection baseline

Use the Siemens 7UM622 documented settings where available.

B. Academic coordination setting

A separate hypothetical 51 study setting can still be explored, but must be labelled:

ENGINEERING STUDY VARIANT — NOT SIEMENS DOCUMENTED SETTING

Do not mix the two.

3. The 15,023.75-A pickup also has a validation problem

The report says GEN-51 is:

1.25 × rated 12,019 A

and then says the minimum phase-fault test uses 43.75886 kA.

That is not the correct way to demonstrate relay sensitivity.

A relay does not see the total fault-current magnitude at the bus.

It sees the current passing through its CT.

This distinction is actually exposed by the report's own results:

total F1 LG is only about 7.27 A
yet the report later refers to 8,414 A as a "phase-branch" quantity
and GEN-51 is said to have NO-TRIP for the unbalanced generator faults.

The reported 8.4-kA quantity is particularly suspicious because it is of roughly the same scale as the generator's prefault current, not the 7.27-A fault current. It needs to be traced back to the exact Phase-4 column and renamed.

For a protection pickup test, the correct logic is:

$$ I_{\text{relay,seen}} = \left|I_{\text{branch through the relay CT}}\right| $$

not

$$ I_{\text{fault,total}} $$
This means the current V9 "minimum phase-fault margin" is not sufficient proof.

You can have:

$$ I_{fault,total}=43.8\text{ kA} $$

while

$$ I_{GEN-CT}<I_{pickup} $$

and the generator relay does not operate.

That is exactly why the report later finds GEN-51 blind to unbalanced faults.

Correction

Replace the current minimum-detect test with:

For every relay, determine the minimum current through that relay's CT for each fault relevant to its protection/backup zone.

This should be done separately for:

phase OC
residual/earth OC
negative sequence
differential, where applicable.
4. GEN-51N = 5 A is not an actual plant setting

Phase 5 uses:

$$ I_{pickup}=5A\ primary $$

which becomes only:

$$ 5/15000=0.333\text{ mA secondary} $$

and detects the 7.27-A generator-terminal ground fault.

Mathematically, that conversion is fine.

Physically, though, this is not established as the plant's actual 51N setting.

The real SLD contains several different generator earth-fault functions, including 51N, 59N and 64G, and the Siemens protection report describes a 100% stator-earth-fault scheme using 20-Hz voltage injection.

The Siemens report also documents:

90% stator earth fault via displacement voltage, ANSI 59N
100% stator earth fault via 20-Hz injection, ANSI 64G
specific current/voltage thresholds for the injected system.

Therefore:

7.27-A system earth-fault current ≠ complete model of generator stator-earth protection.

The 64G scheme cannot be represented simply as:

3I0 > 5 A → relay trips

because its operating principle is different.

Correction

Keep the 5-A element only as:

GEN-51N generic residual-current study sensitivity

unless the actual 51N input/CT/core and setting are established.

Separately document:

51N
59N
64G

as different physical functions.

Do not use the 5-A 51N study as proof that the plant's 100% stator-earth-fault protection works.

5. The 50/51 backup protection is not the main protection for the major faults

This is where the physical SLD changes the interpretation of the Phase-5 results.

F1 — generator internal fault

Actual physical protection includes generator differential 87G.

The Siemens report gives:

87G pickup ≈ 0.20 I/In
high-set ≈ 5.0 I/In
0-s time stages
stabilizing slopes.

So an internal generator fault should primarily be addressed by the differential protection, not by waiting for the 51 backup element at ~0.53 s or 3 s.

Phase 5 currently makes GEN-51 look like the meaningful protection path. It isn't.

F2 — GSUT-side fault

The real transformer protection includes transformer differential and other transformer protections.

A generic GSUT-HV-51 is therefore a backup protection layer, not the main fault-clearing mechanism.

F3 — 230-kV GIS bus fault

This is even more important.

The plant SLD shows 87B busbar protection and 50BF. The project master data identifies Siemens 7SS523 busbar protection.

So for an F3 bus fault:

87B is the physically relevant primary protection.

Phase 5 instead evaluates GIS-Q0-51.

That means a statement such as:

"GIS-Q0-51 operates in X seconds for F3"

does not tell you the actual bus-fault clearing time of the physical plant.

You need to show:

F3 bus fault → 87B → relevant breaker trip(s) → 50BF if breaker fails

F4 — 230-kV line fault

The physical source set identifies 2 × Siemens 7SD5221 line differential protection.

So the first protection question for F4 is:

Does 7SD5221 detect the line fault and trip the relevant breaker(s)?

The current Phase-5 model does not answer that.

It has only:

GIS-Q0-51

and a LINE-21 note.

A line-fault TCC based only on Q0 51 is therefore not a physical line-protection study.

6. Q0 is not the only breaker in the actual plant

This is another significant topology issue.

The Phase-5 report explicitly makes:

Q0 = 52-1 = only duty-eligible breaker.

But the physical protection SLD clearly contains 52G, the generator circuit breaker, as well as 52-1(Q0).

Therefore a physically meaningful protection study must distinguish at least:

52G — generator breaker

and

52-1/Q0 — GIS-side breaker

The current Phase-5 model cannot fully represent generator protection trip paths without that distinction.

What cannot currently be determined

From the available files, we cannot safely determine the complete plant-specific trip matrix such as:

which fault causes 52G only,
which fault trips 52G + Q0,
which transformer lockout trips which breakers,
exact 86 lockout logic,
breaker-failure initiation and backup trip path.

The master data request itself identifies the protection philosophy/trip matrix and breaker timings as missing.

So this part should remain NOT DETERMINABLE FROM AVAILABLE DATA rather than being inferred.

7. The CT assumptions need correction

This is a real Phase-5 data problem.

The report uses:

GSUT-HV-51 CT = 2000/1
GIS-Q0-51 CT = 2000/1

and labels them engineering assumptions.

But the physical project source set contains documented GIS CT information of:

1600/800/400 : 1 A

and the protection SLD also shows 1600/1-A CT quantities in the relevant protection circuitry.

Therefore 2000/1 cannot continue to be treated as the default plant CT.

The exact CT core used for each protection function still has to be mapped from the SLD, because a multi-ratio CT may have different protection/metering cores.

Correct approach

Create:

physical_CT_ratio

selected_CT_core

protection_function

source

study_CT_ratio

and explicitly map them.

Do not simply replace every 2000/1 with 1600/1 without checking the drawing.

8. The 16,000/1 sensitivity is too broadly described

The report says the legacy 16,000/1 sensitivity is fenced.

That is good practice.

But the 16,000/1 conflict is associated with the generator-side CT information, not a blanket alternative for every CT in the plant.

So the sensitivity should mean:

generator CT 15,000/1 versus legacy generator CT 16,000/1

not:

substitute 16,000/1 into every Phase-5 protection device.

That distinction needs to be enforced in code.

9. The coordination failures are not "plant protection failures"

This is extremely important for your final report.

Phase 5 obtains:

FAIL = 20
NO-TRIP = 28
NO-PAIR = 24
NOT DETERMINABLE = 24
PASS = 0.

The report correctly says these are results under study settings. Good.

But because the settings are largely assumed:

GEN TMS = 0.1
GSUT TMS = 0.2
GIS TMS = 0.3
SI curve
CTI = 0.3 s

these FAILs cannot be interpreted as "the Ashuganj plant protection is badly coordinated."

The Siemens report explicitly says that the generator backup O/C time and curve need the grid time-grading plan/customer information for correct setting.

Therefore the proper conclusion is:

"The assumed study settings do not achieve the selected 0.3-s coordination criterion in the qualified model."

Not:

"The actual plant relays fail coordination."

10. The 0.3-s CTI is reasonable as an academic assumption — but not plant-specific

Your 0.3-s grading margin is a perfectly reasonable starting engineering assumption for a university study.

The EEE 305 material itself teaches relay/circuit-breaker selection and protection coordination concepts, but it does not provide Ashuganj-specific coordination data.

So keep:

CTI = 0.3 s — ENGINEERING ASSUMPTION

but don't present it as:

Ashuganj actual coordination margin = 0.3 s.

11. The breaker-duty section needs a wording correction

The report says:

40 rows are NOT DETERMINABLE because no Q0 interrupting rating is sourced.

This is partly right, but too broad.

Your physical GIS source material already identifies:

230-kV GIS
3150 A
50 kA
physical GIS protection
documented equipment information.

However, there is an important distinction:

Available

GIS short-time withstand / equipment 50-kA figure

Not yet established

Q0 breaker-specific interrupting/breaking capability and complete breaker-duty basis

Therefore the correct wording is not:

"50 kA rating missing."

It should be:

"A 50-kA GIS equipment withstand value is documented, but a Q0-specific interrupting/breaking rating and complete duty basis are not established from the supplied evidence."

Also, your F3:

$$ 50.53\text{ kA} $$

versus

$$ 50\text{ kA} $$

should be discussed as a potential equipment-duty concern, but not declared FAIL because the exact duty category, duration, breaker rating and interruption basis are not established.

12. 50-kA has two different meanings and Phase 5 should separate them

There are two concepts floating around:

System fault-level reference

Approximately 50 kA, used in the Phase-4 grid equivalent and identified as estimated.

GIS equipment rating

Approximately 50 kA, appearing in the plant equipment documentation.

Those are not the same thing.

Your Phase-5 report needs two separate fields:

I_fault_system_reference

and

equipment_short_circuit_rating

Otherwise a reader may think the calculated fault level was independently measured against the breaker rating.

13. The TCC plots are currently not physical plant TCCs

The report calls them:

generator-zone TCC
grid-zone TCC

but the curves are generic SI curves with assumed TMS values.

For the generator, that is especially misleading because the Siemens report says inverse overcurrent protection is disabled for the actual generator relay.

The generator TCC should therefore have at least two clearly separated modes:

Physical documented generator protection

versus

Generic study backup overcurrent protection

Otherwise your evaluator can quite reasonably ask:

"Why is your TCC showing an inverse relay when the Siemens protection report says inverse O/C is disabled?"

And that would be a valid criticism.

14. Your low-earth-fault result is useful, but its protection interpretation is wrong

The Phase-4 physics itself is valuable:

$$ I_{F1,LG}\approx7.27A $$

and the neutral impedance is correctly carried through the fault calculation.

Phase 5 then proves:

$$ 7.27A \rightarrow 0.4848mA $$

through a 15,000/1 CT.

That arithmetic is fine.

But saying this proves the plant earth-fault protection works is too strong.

The actual generator protection architecture contains:

51N
59N
64G 100% stator earth fault
rotor earth protection
50BF

with different measurement principles.

So your result should be titled something like:

"Residual-current backup earth-fault study under the qualified 51N assumption"

rather than:

"Generator earth-fault protection validated."

15. One especially suspicious data item: 8.414 kA

This deserves a direct code audit.

The report says:

phase-branch = 8414.12 A

while simultaneously describing F1 LG as a 7.272-A total earth fault.

If 8414.12 A is intended to be the current actually passing through the generator phase CT during that F1 LG fault, that is physically inconsistent with the 7.272-A LG result.

It may turn out to be:

a prefault branch-current quantity,
a sequence component,
a frozen load-flow anchor,
or another Phase-4 contribution field.

But the report currently calls it a phase-branch quantity without adequately defining it.

This should be investigated before Phase 5 is considered physically closed.
16. What the EEE 305 slides tell us — and what they don't

The EEE 305 material is useful for checking the protection-study methodology, not the actual Ashuganj plant settings.

The course explicitly covers:

fault levels
circuit-breaker selection
relays/circuit breakers
symmetrical and unsymmetrical faults
power plants
substation layouts.

The bus-configuration slides also show why breaker/disconnector/bus-coupler distinctions matter. In the main-and-transfer-bus material, the bus coupler is used for transferring a circuit between buses; the slides distinguish isolators from circuit breakers and describe the switching sequence.

That supports keeping your Q0/Q1/Q2/Q9 semantics correct.

But the 305 slides are not evidence that Ashuganj itself uses the exact illustrated arrangement or relay settings. The actual plant SLD has to control that, and the actual SLD shows a much more detailed protection scheme.

17. What is actually correct in Phase 5

There is quite a lot that should be retained.

Component	Assessment
Phase-4 read-only adapter	✅ Correct
No Phase-3/4 rewriting	✅ Correct
Machine-readable outputs	✅ Correct
CT arithmetic itself	✅ Correct
Legacy CT fencing concept	✅ Correct
Separate breaker-duty engine	✅ Correct
No invented breaker verdict	✅ Correct in principle
0.3-s CTI labelled as assumption	✅ Correct
Explicit NO-PAIR / NOT-DETERMINABLE states	✅ Good
Refusing to tune settings until PASS	✅ Very good
Provenance tags	✅ Good
344/0 tests	✅ Good implementation evidence
16/16 validation	✅ Good implementation evidence

The implementation discipline is actually one of the strongest parts of the report.

18. What needs to be corrected — priority order
P0 — Must correct before calling Phase 5 physically aligned

1. Replace 2000/1 CT assumptions where actual CT information exists.

2. Separate physical protection from generic 51/51N study protection.

3. Correct GEN-51 to the actual Siemens documented configuration:
50/51 I> with inverse disabled; documented pickup ≈17.171 kA / 1.14 A secondary; 3-s time marked for coordination confirmation.

4. Replace the current "minimum fault detection" validation with minimum current through the relay CT.

5. Audit the 8.414-kA F1 LG "phase-branch" quantity.

6. Add the actual 52G generator breaker to the topology/protection registry.

7. Reclassify 87G, 87B, 7SD5221, transformer 87/87N, 64G, 59N, 46, 21 and 50BF as the actual primary/major protection functions.

P1 — Strongly recommended

Add separate physical protection zones:

GENERATOR ZONE
    87G / 46 / 64G / 59N / 51 backup
         |
        52G
         |
      GSUT
    87 / 63 / 49 / backup 51
         |
        Q0
         |
    230-kV GIS BUS
       87B / 50BF
         |
      LINE BAY
   7SD5221 x 2 / 21 backup
         |
     South Line
         |
    Remote Grid

This is much closer to the real plant documentation.

P2 — Then improve coordination

After the physical zones are established:

use documented Siemens generator settings where available;
use generic settings only where actual settings are missing;
calculate relay currents from the correct CT core;
coordinate backup 51 elements;
separately calculate primary differential/line/bus protection operation where the necessary inputs exist;
do not convert "20 FAILs" into "plant failures."
19. What still genuinely cannot be determined

These should remain explicitly unresolved unless better source documents arrive:

Item	Status
Q0-specific interrupting/breaking rating	Not established
Complete Q0 breaker opening/interrupting duty basis	Not established
Complete physical trip matrix	Not established
Actual as-left relay settings	Not established
Complete GSUT/GIS CT core-to-relay mapping	Needs confirmation from SLD/test documents
CT knee point/burden/ALF/secondary lead burden	Incomplete
Actual line 7SD5221 settings	Not available
Actual distance-21 reaches/timers	Not available
Remote-end line relay settings	Not available
Remote-grid equivalent protection	Not available
Exact GIS 87B settings	Not available
GIS 50BF settings	Not available
Exact GAT/UAT relay settings	Not fully available
Commissioned/approved protection settings	Not established
Exact generator 51 timing after customer coordination	Siemens source itself marks timing ??
Actual 64G commissioning settings	Not fully established
Breaker mechanical opening time	Missing
CT saturation behavior under faults	Not determinable from present data

The project master data itself identifies missing protection philosophy, relay settings, CT test data, and breaker timing information, so these are legitimate data gaps rather than things we should invent.

20. How I would characterize Phase 5 right now

I would not throw Phase 5 away.

The right correction is to change the architecture from:

"Ashuganj South protection coordination model"

to something closer to:

"Ashuganj South protection application framework with a validated backup overcurrent/earth-fault study layer and source-mapped physical protection architecture."

Then the next correction stream should make the physical plant protection architecture authoritative, while preserving your generic coordination engine as a separate study layer.

That gives you a much more defensible engineering report:

Primary protection

87G / 87 transformer / 87B / 7SD5221 / 64G / 59N / 46 / 21 etc.

Backup protection

51 / 51N / transformer backup OC etc.

What Phase 5 quantitatively coordinates

Primarily the backup OC layer, unless enough source data exists to model the primary function.

What cannot be claimed

Actual commissioned coordination, actual relay settings, exact breaker duty compliance.

Master correction prompt for the implementation agent
PHASE-5 PHYSICAL ALIGNMENT CORRECTION — MANDATORY

Do NOT rebuild Phase 5 from scratch.

Keep the existing Phase-4 adapter architecture, validation framework,
provenance system, production writer, and read-only freeze.

The objective is to correct the Phase-5 protection model so that it
matches the PHYSICAL ASHUGANJ SOUTH protection documentation wherever
source evidence exists, while keeping generic study assumptions clearly
separated.

============================================================
1. RECLASSIFY THE STUDY
============================================================

Change the primary scope description from a generic "plant protection
coordination study" to:

"Physical protection architecture + qualified backup overcurrent/earth-
fault coordination study."

Do not claim that all plant protection functions have been simulated.

============================================================
2. IMPORT THE PHYSICAL PROTECTION ARCHITECTURE
============================================================

Create a source-backed protection registry containing at minimum:

GENERATOR:
- 87G
- 46
- 40
- 32R
- 21
- 78
- 59
- 81
- 24
- 59N
- 64G
- 50/27
- 50BF
- 51 / 51N

GENERATOR BREAKER:
- 52G

GSUT:
- 87 / transformer differential
- 87N where supported
- 63
- 49
- 50/51 backup
- 50BF
- 86 trip/lockout path where documented

UAT/GAT:
- documented transformer protection functions
- differential / earth / overcurrent / thermal / lockout as supported

230-kV GIS:
- 87B busbar protection
- 50BF
- Q0 / 52-1
- Q1/Q2/Q9 disconnectors
- other documented protection functions

230-kV LINE:
- Siemens 7SD5221 x2
- 21 only where actual/settings data are available

Do not assign invented settings to these functions.

============================================================
3. CT CORRECTION
============================================================

Do not use 2000/1 as a blanket physical CT assumption.

Use source-backed CT information from the project protection SLD/master
data.

Document:
- CT ratio
- core
- function
- location
- source
- whether exact function-core mapping is confirmed

Where exact core selection is not established, mark it
NOT DETERMINABLE FROM AVAILABLE DATA.

The 16000/1 legacy sensitivity applies only to the generator CT conflict
where supported. Do not replace all plant CTs with 16000/1.

============================================================
4. GENERATOR 51 MUST MATCH THE SIEMENS DOCUMENTED BASELINE
============================================================

The Siemens generator protection report states:

- 50/51 I> ON
- inverse O/C disabled
- I> = 1.14 A secondary
- equivalent primary setting ≈ 17,171 A
- time delay = 3.00 s, but marked ?? and requiring coordination
  information.

Therefore:

Create a SOURCE-BACKED SIEMENS-BASELINE protection entry using these
values.

Do NOT represent this source-backed generator protection as an IEC
Standard Inverse curve with TMS=0.1.

Keep the existing IEC-SI generator setting only as:

ENGINEERING STUDY VARIANT

and ensure it is visually and numerically separated from the Siemens
baseline.

============================================================
5. GENERATOR 51 PICKUP VALIDATION
============================================================

Delete/replace any validation that claims generator relay sensitivity
using TOTAL BUS FAULT CURRENT.

For every relay:

    minimum_detectable_current =
    minimum current THROUGH THAT RELAY'S CT

Perform this separately for:

- F1/F2/F3/F4/F5
- LLL
- LG
- LL
- LLG
- each operating case

Use actual branch/through-current quantities from Phase-4.

Do not use total fault level as a proxy for relay current.

============================================================
6. AUDIT THE 8414-A F1-LG QUANTITY
============================================================

Trace the exact Phase-4 source column producing the reported
8414.12-A "phase-branch" quantity.

Determine whether it is:

- prefault current
- branch contribution
- sequence quantity
- fault-phase current
- another quantity

It must not be labelled "fault phase branch current" unless KCL and
sequence identities support that interpretation.

Add an automated test against the Phase-4 fault-current/contribution
dataset.

============================================================
7. EARTH-FAULT FUNCTIONS MUST BE SEPARATED
============================================================

Do not claim that a 5-A generic 51N study represents all generator
earth-fault protection.

Maintain separate physical-function entries:

- 51N residual OC
- 59N stator-earth displacement voltage
- 64G 100% stator-earth protection using the documented 20-Hz injection
  principle
- 64R rotor-earth protection

Use the existing 5-A 51N only as an:

ENGINEERING STUDY VARIANT / SENSITIVE EARTH-FAULT CASE

unless the actual 51N setting is sourced.

Never use the 5-A result as proof of 64G operation.

============================================================
8. PRIMARY PROTECTION ZONES
============================================================

Build explicit zone mapping:

Zone G:
generator stator
87G / 46 / 64G / 59N / backup 51

Zone T:
GSUT
87 / 87N / 63 / 49 / backup 51

Zone B:
230-kV GIS bus
87B / 50BF

Zone L:
230-kV line
7SD5221 x2 / distance 21 where supported

Do not use the chain:

GEN-51 -> GSUT-51 -> GIS-51

as though it were the physical primary protection chain.

That chain may remain as a BACKUP-OVERCURRENT study path only.

============================================================
9. GENERATOR BREAKER
============================================================

Add physical breaker 52G to the protection topology.

Do not invent the exact trip matrix.

Where the trip path is uncertain, record:

TRIP MATRIX = NOT DETERMINABLE FROM AVAILABLE DATA

Do not assume which lockout trips Q0 versus 52G without source evidence.

============================================================
10. GIS BUS FAULT
============================================================

For F3, identify:

PRIMARY:
87B

BACKUP:
GIS-Q0-51 or other documented backup function

Do not treat Q0-51 operation as the busbar primary-clearing time.

If 87B settings are unavailable, report:

87B PRIMARY OPERATION = NOT DETERMINABLE

rather than substituting 51 time.

============================================================
11. LINE FAULT
============================================================

For F4:

PRIMARY:
7SD5221 line differential

SECONDARY/BACKUP:
21 / 51 where source-supported

Do not call GIS-Q0-51 the physical line primary protection.

Because actual 7SD settings are missing, mark exact operating time
NOT DETERMINABLE.

============================================================
12. BREAKER DUTY
============================================================

Separate:

A. GIS equipment short-time withstand
B. Q0 interrupting/breaking capability

Use the documented 50-kA GIS equipment value as SOURCE-BACKED equipment
information.

Do not automatically call that the Q0 interrupting rating.

If Q0-specific interrupting capability is not established:

Q0 INTERRUPTING DUTY = NOT DETERMINABLE

Do not remove the source-backed GIS 50-kA value from the report.

============================================================
13. TCC FIGURES
============================================================

Generate two clearly distinct classes of plots:

A. PHYSICAL/SOURCE-BACKED PROTECTION CHARACTERISTICS
where enough source information exists.

B. GENERIC BACKUP OC STUDY CHARACTERISTICS
for engineering-assumption relays.

Do not show the generic IEC-SI GEN-51 curve as if it were the Siemens
7UM622 plant setting.

============================================================
14. COORDINATION VERDICTS
============================================================

Keep the 0.3-s CTI as:

ENGINEERING ASSUMPTION

Do NOT describe FAIL rows as physical plant protection failures.

Use wording:

"Study-setting coordination shortfall"

rather than:

"Plant protection failure"

unless actual plant settings are sourced and checked.

============================================================
15. PRIMARY VS BACKUP EFFECTIVENESS TABLE
============================================================

For every required fault case, generate:

Fault
Primary protection function
Primary protection availability
Primary operating time
Backup protection function
Backup operating time
CT source
Setting source
Detection status
What is determinable
What is not determinable

This table is mandatory.

============================================================
16. PHYSICAL PROTECTION EFFECTIVENESS
============================================================

Explain how the actual documented functions protect the plant:

87G:
fast selective generator internal-fault protection

46:
negative-sequence/unbalance protection

64G/59N:
generator stator earth-fault coverage

21:
impedance-based backup/fault detection

87 transformer:
internal transformer faults

87B:
230-kV busbar faults

7SD5221:
line faults

50BF:
breaker failure backup

51:
backup overcurrent

Do not fabricate times where source settings are unavailable.

============================================================
17. REQUIRED VALIDATION ADDITIONS
============================================================

Add tests for:

- physical CT mapping
- generator 15k/16k sensitivity scope
- GEN-51 Siemens baseline
- GEN-51 generic study variant separation
- relay current = branch-through-current, not total fault current
- 52G presence
- 87G/87B/7SD physical zone mapping
- F3 primary = 87B
- F4 primary = 7SD
- 51N vs 64G separation
- GIS 50-kA equipment rating vs Q0 interrupting rating separation
- 8414-A quantity traceability
- no protection-result source conflation

============================================================
18. REPORT LANGUAGE
============================================================

The final report must explicitly separate:

SOURCE-BACKED PHYSICAL PROTECTION
ENGINEERING STUDY PROTECTION
LEGACY SENSITIVITY
DERIVED RESULT
NOT DETERMINABLE

Never call study settings:
"actual plant settings"
"commissioned settings"
"Siemens settings"

unless directly supported.

============================================================
19. FINAL ACCEPTANCE CONDITION
============================================================

Phase 5 is physically aligned only when:

[ ] 52G is represented
[ ] physical protection functions are mapped
[ ] CT mapping is corrected
[ ] GEN-51 Siemens baseline is separated from generic study OC
[ ] minimum-detect tests use relay branch current
[ ] 51N is separated from 64G/59N
[ ] 87G/87B/7SD primary roles are represented
[ ] breaker-duty rating semantics are corrected
[ ] 20 coordination FAILs are clearly labelled study-setting findings
[ ] no unsupported plant protection time is claimed
[ ] all unresolved data gaps remain explicitly NOT DETERMINABLE
[ ] Phase-4 remains completely read-only
[ ] all automated tests pass
Bottom line

Do not proceed to another phase yet. Correct Phase 5 first.

The software framework is in good shape, but the protection engineering layer needs one significant correction pass because the actual plant documents show that the real system is based on generator differential/earth/negative-sequence/impedance protection, transformer differential, GIS busbar protection, breaker-failure protection and dual line-differential protection, with 51/51N acting mainly as backup functions.

The single biggest numerical correction is the GEN-51 implementation, and the single biggest architectural correction is to introduce the actual physical protection zones and 52G/Q0/87G/87B/7SD5221 relationships before interpreting coordination results.
Verifying specific protection settings and equipment data against provided source documents before proceeding.
Auditing source semantics for the 8.414kA value and mapping relay totals versus branch currents.

<skill_content name="brainstorming">
# Skill: brainstorming

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by classifying how much process the request needs, then work
through your path: understand the context, refine the idea, present a
design, and get your human partner's approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any
project, or take any implementation action until you have told your
human partner what you intend and they have approved it. This applies
to EVERY task on EVERY path below — the ceremony scales with the task;
the approval gate never does.
</HARD-GATE>

## Three Paths

Before your first question, classify the request and say the
classification out loud — "this looks bounded, so I'll present a short
design here rather than write a spec" — so your human partner can
override it:

- **Spike** — a feasibility question ("can we...", "is it possible...",
  "quick and dirty is fine") whose output is an answer, not code you
  keep. Present the question and what you'll try in 2-3 sentences, get
  a nod, then find out as cheaply as correctness allows. No design
  doc, no spec file. Report findings as a recommendation; anything you
  built stays labeled throwaway.
- **Bounded** — a well-scoped change to code that already exists in
  this repo: a new flag, a small endpoint, a one-file fix.
  Understanding the kind of app is not enough — bounded means the flow
  you are changing is already here to read. If there is no existing
  flow to change, the task is not bounded. Ask the clarifying
  questions that matter, present a short design IN CHAT (a few
  sentences to a few short paragraphs), and STOP. Implementation
  starts only after your human partner says yes to that design — a
  bounded task's approval is as hard a gate as an architectural
  one. No spec file, no implementation plan document.
- **Architectural** — new projects, new subsystems, changes that
  restructure how components fit together or alter interfaces others
  depend on. Follow the full process: questions, approaches, sectioned
  design, written spec, then the writing-plans skill.

When in doubt between two paths, take the heavier one. The ratchet is
one-way: hidden complexity discovered mid-task upgrades the path —
stop, say so, and step up. Nothing downgrades mid-task.

## Anti-Pattern: "Too Simple To Need Approval"

Every path ends with your human partner approving your intent before
implementation. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config
change — the design may be two sentences in chat, but you MUST present
it and get approval. "Simple" tasks are where unexamined assumptions
cause the most wasted work. What scales with simplicity is the
artifact, never the approval.

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "This is too simple to need a design" | Simple means a short design, not no design. Two sentences in chat, then approval. |
| "I'll call it bounded and skip the spec" | Reaching for a label to skip work IS the doubt — take the heavier path. |
| "It's bounded and the design is obvious — I'll start while they read it" | The gate is the approval, not the design's length. Present, then stop until you hear yes. |
| "I understand this kind of app, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the repo, not your familiarity. A new project has no existing flow — it is architectural. |
| "The spike works, so I'll keep the code" | A spike's output is an answer. Keeping the code is a new request — classify it. |
| "It grew, but I'm almost done — no need to re-classify" | Hidden complexity upgrades the path mid-task. Stop and say so. |
| "They approved the spike, so the follow-up change is approved too" | Each task gets its own classification and its own approval. |

## Checklist

Classify first, announce the path, then create a task for each item on
your path and complete them in order.

**Spike:**
1. **Explore project context** — enough to frame the probe
2. **Present question + probe plan** — 2-3 sentences
3. **Get approval** — a nod is enough
4. **Investigate** — as cheaply as correctness allows
5. **Report findings** — a recommendation; label anything built as throwaway

**Bounded:**
1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, the ones that matter
3. **Present short design in chat** — approach, files touched, testing
4. **Get approval** — STOP and wait for an explicit yes; presenting the design and starting in the same breath is skipping the gate
5. **Implement** — proceed with the normal development workflow (TDD applies); no plan document

**Architectural:**
1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer the visual companion just-in-time** — NOT upfront. The first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than described, offer it then (its own message); on approval its browser tab opens for you. If no visual question ever arises, never offer it. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## Process Flow

```dot
digraph brainstorming {
    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" [shape=diamond];
    "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" [shape=box];
    "Present short design in chat" [shape=box];
    "Human approves?" [shape=diamond];
    "Investigate; report recommendation" [shape=doublecircle];
    "Implement via normal workflow (no plan doc)" [shape=doublecircle];
    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
    "Present design sections" [shape=box];
    "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
    "Write design doc" [shape=box];
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" [shape=box];
    "User reviews spec?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke writing-plans skill" [shape=doublecircle];
    "Hidden complexity? Upgrade path" [shape=box];

    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" [label="spike"];
    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" [label="bounded"];
    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Explore project context" [label="architectural"];
    "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" -> "Human approves?";
    "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" -> "Present short design in chat";
    "Present short design in chat" -> "Human approves?";
    "Human approves?" -> "Investigate; report recommendation" [label="spike: yes"];
    "Human approves?" -> "Implement via normal workflow (no plan doc)" [label="bounded: yes"];
    "Hidden complexity? Upgrade path" -> "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural";
    "Explore project context" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
    "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
    "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
    "Write design doc" -> "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)";
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" -> "User reviews spec?";
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Write design doc" [label="changes requested"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Invoke writing-plans skill" [label="approved"];
}
```

**Terminal states are path-bound.** Architectural: the ONLY skill you
invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans — never frontend-design,
mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. Bounded: after
approval, implementation proceeds directly through the normal
development workflow; no plan document. Spike: the terminal state is a
reported recommendation.

## The Process

The subsections below serve the bounded and architectural paths (a
spike stops at "present the probe, get a nod"). Sections from
**Exploring approaches** onward are architectural-path depth — for
bounded work, context plus a few questions plus a short in-chat design
is the whole process.

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why
- YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design (architectural path)

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Self-Review:**
After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:

1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.

Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Visual Companion

# Phase-5b Physical-Alignment Correction — Spec Addendum

**Date:** 2026-09-19
**Status:** Approved (triple approval: USER_ASSERTED_PENDING_DOC + uniform TMS 0.20 + start C1)
**Parent spec:** `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-19-phase5-protection-design.md`
**Parent plan:** `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-09-19-phase5-implementation.md`
**Trigger:** Independent physical review vs protection SLD / Siemens BD1015 report / EEE 305 slides.
**Verdict adopted:** Phase-5 shipped outputs are a disciplined *backup-OC study*, not a faithful
physical-protection model. Correct, don't rebuild. Old production tag frozen untouched; new tag
`production-v2` carries corrected numbers.

## S1. Scope reclassification (binding language)

Primary scope becomes: "Physical protection architecture + qualified backup
overcurrent/earth-fault coordination study." Never claim all plant functions simulated.
Coordination shortfalls are "study-setting coordination shortfalls," never plant failures.
TCCs split into PHYSICAL/SOURCE-BACKED vs GENERIC STUDY classes.

## S2. Source ledger (workspace-verified; transcribed in C1)

Master §§17–21 (Q0/Q1/Q2/Q9/Q51/Q52/Q8; CT 1600/800/400:1 multi-core; 7SD5221×2; 7SS523;
6MD66; OC 51 = 1.20×max-load / IEC SI / TMS 0.20 initial / 51N 0.20 A sec / TMS 0.15 /
grading 0.3 s CTI / transformer diff 0.30 pu-30%-60% / gen diff start 0.20 pu — all Status C
starting assumptions); Siemens pp.6–7 (15000/1 T1+T2 cores; 458 MVA/22 kV/12019 A/Imax 14309 A/
I2max 7.64 %/K 7.41 s/NER 60 Ω+2.62 Ω??/grid 50 kA estimated/VT residual 381.05);

12.4 kA/100 kA sym breaking; 7UT6331 transformer diff; GIS 8DN9 bays 2000 A / busbars+coup

clearing ENGINEER_DERIVED). Absent from workspace: Siemens pp.8–39 (all 7UM622 function

## S3. Provenance class added: USER_ASSERTED_PENDING_DOC

(7UM622 50/51 I> ON, inverse disabled, I> = 1.14 A secondary ≈ 17,171 A primary,

## S4. CT correction (replaces 2000/1 blanket)

default bay connection + rating-plate corroboration). Registry gains physical_CT_ratio,
selected_CT_core, protection_function, study_CT_ratio columns; exact function-core

GAT/UAT CTs (GAT HV-N 250/1 T6, T1 dual 500,250/1 tap UNKNOWN; UAT HV 1000/1) mapped for
zone completeness. Legacy-16000/1 sensitivity narrowed to generator CT conflict only
(never substituted into non-generator devices).

## S5. Two-layer generator protection

PHYSICAL baseline GEN-51-SIEMENS-BL: definite-time I>, Is = 17,171 A primary
(1.1447 A secondary, USER_ASSERTED_PENDING_DOC + DERIVED cross-check), tdef = 3.00 s

breaker_interrupting_rating (52G/GCB-10BAC10 100 kA sym breaking, SOURCE-BACKED

No TBD/TODO (USER_ASSERTED_PENDING_DOC is a defined state with promotion rule, not a

# Skill: writing-plans

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Task Right-Sizing

A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
independently testable deliverable.

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

**Spec:** [path to the spec/design doc this plan implements — the plan
argues from the spec, so the spec travels with it; executors read both]

## Global Constraints

[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
include this section.]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter
  and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this
  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Write minimal implementation**

```python
def function(input):
    return expected
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## No Placeholders

Every step must contain the actual content an engineer needs. These are **plan failures** — never write them:
- "TBD", "TODO", "implement later", "fill in details"
- "Add appropriate error handling" / "add validation" / "handle edge cases"
- "Write tests for the above" (without actual test code)
- "Similar to Task N" (repeat the code — the engineer may be reading tasks out of order)
- Steps that describe what to do without showing how (code blocks required for code steps)
- References to types, functions, or methods not defined in any task

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Placeholder scan:** Search your plan for red flags — any of the patterns from the "No Placeholders" section above. Fix them.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving the plan, offer execution choice:

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Two execution options:**

**1. Subagent-Driven (recommended)** - I dispatch a fresh subagent per task, review between tasks, fast iteration

**2. Inline Execution** - Execute tasks in this session using executing-plans, batch execution with checkpoints

**Which approach?"**

**If Subagent-Driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development
- Fresh subagent per task + two-stage review

**If Inline Execution chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans
- Batch execution with checkpoints for review

<skill_content name="subagent-driven-development">
# Skill: subagent-driven-development

# Subagent-Driven Development

Execute plan by dispatching a fresh implementer subagent per task, a task review (spec compliance + code quality) after each, and a broad whole-branch review at the end.

**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + task review (spec + quality) + broad final review = high quality, fast iteration

**Narration:** between tool calls, narrate at most one short line — the
ledger and the tool results carry the record.

**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner between tasks. Execute all tasks from the plan without stopping. The only reasons to stop are the four named below, or all tasks complete. "Should I continue?" prompts and progress summaries waste their time — they asked you to execute the plan, so execute it.

**Rulings, not stalls.** A running plan does not wait on a human. Conflicts,
ambiguities, plan defects, a cap you would have asked to exceed — decide
them. The spec is the binding authority, the plan is its argument, and your
judgment settles what neither answers. Record every decision in the ledger as
`Ruling: <what you decided> — <why> — <what it costs if wrong>`, and keep
going. A wrong ruling costs rework your human partner can see and undo; a
session parked on a question costs their whole day and buys nothing.

Four things stop you, and only these: an irreversible or destructive
operation; a security-sensitive action; a side effect outside this worktree
that norms say you ask about first (a merge, a push to a shared branch, a
publish); and a plan so broken that every path forward is a guess. For those,
stop and ask.

## When to Use

```dot

    "Have implementation plan?" [shape=diamond];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" [shape=diamond];
    "Stay in this session?" [shape=diamond];
    "subagent-driven-development" [shape=box];

    "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [shape=box];

    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Tasks mostly independent?" [label="yes"];
    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no"];

    "Stay in this session?" -> "subagent-driven-development" [label="yes"];
    "Stay in this session?" -> "executing-plans" [label="no - parallel session"];
}
```

**vs. Executing Plans (parallel session):**
- Same session (no context switch)
- Fresh subagent per task (no context pollution)
- Review after each task (spec compliance + code quality), broad review at the end
- Faster iteration (no human-in-loop between tasks)
