## Setup

Ensure the work happens in an isolated workspace: use
superpowers:using-git-worktrees to create one or verify the existing one.
Never start implementation on a main/master branch without your human
partner's explicit consent.

Conversation memory does not survive compaction. In real sessions,
controllers that lost their place have re-dispatched entire completed task
sequences — the single most expensive failure observed. Track progress in
a ledger file, not only in todos.

- Each plan owns a workspace: at skill start, run this skill's
  `scripts/sdd-workspace PLAN_FILE` — it prints the plan's git-ignored
  directory (`<repo-root>/.superpowers/sdd/<plan-basename>/`), home to
  every artifact for THIS plan: ledger, briefs, reports, review packages.
  Another plan's directory is never yours to read or write.
- Check for this plan's ledger at `<workspace>/progress.md`. If its first
  line names your plan file, tasks with a `Task <N>: complete` line are DONE
  — do not re-dispatch them; resume at the first task without one. A task
  whose last line is a fix round is mid-loop: resume the loop at the next
  round. A ledger whose first line names a different plan file — or a stray
  ledger at the old flat path `.superpowers/sdd/progress.md` — is another
  plan's progress: leave it in place and start your own, fresh.
- Create the ledger with its identity as the first line:
  `# SDD ledger — plan: <plan file path>`.
- The ledger is your recovery map: the commits it names exist in git even
  when your context no longer remembers creating them. After compaction,
  trust the ledger and `git log` over your own recollection.
- `git clean -fdx` will destroy the workspace (it's git-ignored scratch); if
  that happens, recover from `git log`.

Read the plan once, note its context and Global Constraints, and create a
todo per task. If the plan names a Spec, read that too: the spec is the
authority the plan argues from, and conflicts inside the plan resolve
against it. A plan with no reachable spec gets a ledger note saying so —
rulings made without one are provisional.

Before dispatching Task 1, scan the plan once for conflicts, writing down
what you checked as you check it:

- tasks that contradict each other or the plan's Global Constraints
- anything the plan explicitly mandates that the review rubric treats as a
  defect (a test that asserts nothing, verbatim duplication of a logic block)

The scan's output is a table, not a verdict. One row for every pair of tasks
that share a file or an interface: the two tasks, what one produces against
what the other consumes, and what you found. One row for every task: whether
its own text agrees with itself — the tests it specifies against the code it
specifies, the files it creates against the files it later touches. "The scan
is clean" without those rows is not a scan you ran.

Write the table to the ledger. Rule on everything you find before execution
begins — each finding against the plan text that mandates it — and record
each ruling in the ledger. If the scan is clean, proceed without comment.
Rule on each conflict it surfaces — the spec is the binding authority, the
plan is its argument — record the ruling beside its row, and dispatch
Task 1. The review loop remains the net for conflicts that only emerge from
implementation.

## Model Selection

Use the least powerful model that can handle each role to conserve cost and increase speed.

**Mechanical implementation tasks** (isolated functions, clear specs, 1-2 files): use a fast, cheap model. Most implementation tasks are mechanical when the plan is well-specified.

**Integration and judgment tasks** (multi-file coordination, pattern matching, debugging): use a standard model.

**Architecture and design tasks**: use the most capable available model.
The final whole-branch review is one of these — dispatch it on the most
capable available model, not the session default.

**Review tasks**: choose the model with the same judgment, scaled to the
diff's size, complexity, and risk. A small mechanical diff does not need the
most capable model; a subtle concurrency change does. Scoped re-reviews of
small fix diffs take a cheap-to-mid tier.

**Fix-loop escalation (rounds 4-5)**: use a model at least one tier above
the implementer that got stuck.

**Always specify the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent.** An
omitted model inherits your session's model — often the most capable and
most expensive — which silently defeats this section.

**Turn count beats token price.** Wall-clock and context cost scale with how
many turns a subagent takes, and the cheapest models routinely take 2-3× the
turns on multi-step work — costing more overall. Use a mid-tier model as the
floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose descriptions.
When the task's plan text contains the complete code to write, the
implementation is transcription plus testing: use the cheapest tier for
that implementer. Single-file mechanical fixes also take the cheapest tier.

**Task complexity signals (implementation tasks):**
- Touches 1-2 files with a complete spec → cheap model
- Touches multiple files with integration concerns → standard model
- Requires design judgment or broad codebase understanding → most capable model

## The Task Loop

**Batch small same-shape work.** When the plan lists several tasks that are
each a small, independent edit of the same kind — the same one-line fix,
constant change, or field addition repeated across files — do not dispatch
one subagent per task. Compose ONE dispatch brief listing every file and
its change, send the whole batch to a single subagent, and review its diff
as one unit. Reserve one-dispatch-per-task for work that needs its own
judgment, its own tests, or its own review surface.

Everything you paste into a dispatch prompt — and everything a subagent
prints back — stays resident in your context for the rest of the session
and is re-read on every later turn. Hand artifacts over as files.

**Waiting on dispatched subagents:** never poll a wait interface with
short timeouts, and never sit in one silent, open-ended wait either.
While you have local work — ledger updates, packaging the next review,
reading reports — keep working; child results arrive on their own.
When you are genuinely idle, wait in bounded stretches (five to ten
minutes, where your platform allows), and between stretches post one
line of status and reconcile your live children: list them, and chase
any that finished without reporting. A bounded stretch keeps nearly
all of a long wait's efficiency while guaranteeing a stuck or lost
child is noticed within minutes, not at the end of the session.

### 1. Dispatch the implementer

Record BASE (`git rev-parse HEAD`) before dispatching — the review package
and fix-round diffs need it.

- **Task brief:** before dispatching an implementer, run this skill's
  `scripts/task-brief PLAN_FILE N` — it extracts the task's full text to a
  uniquely named file and prints the path. Compose the dispatch so the
  brief stays the single source of
  requirements. Your dispatch should contain: (1) one line on where this
  task fits in the project; (2) the brief path, introduced as "read this
  first — it is your requirements, with the exact values to use verbatim";
  (3) interfaces and decisions from earlier tasks that the brief cannot
  know; (4) your resolution of any ambiguity you noticed in the brief;
  (5) the report-file path and report contract. Exact values (numbers,
  magic strings, signatures, test cases) appear only in the brief. Never
  make a subagent read the whole plan file.
- **Report file:** name the implementer's report file after the brief
  (brief `…/task-N-brief.md` → report `…/task-N-report.md`) and put it in
  the dispatch prompt. The implementer writes the full report there and
  returns only status, commits, a one-line test summary, and concerns.
- A dispatch prompt describes one task, not the session's history. Do not
  paste accumulated prior-task summaries ("state after Tasks 1-3") into
  later dispatches — a real session's dispatch hit 42k chars of which 99%
  was pasted history. A fresh subagent needs its task, the interfaces it
  touches, and the global constraints. Nothing else.
- The dispatch carries the no-subagents contract (it is in the
  implementer template): the implementer never dispatches subagents —
  not helpers, and never a reviewer. Review arrives from you, after the
  report. In real sessions, every reviewer a worker spawned duplicated
  the task review the controller dispatched anyway — a full extra
  review seat per task.
- If an earlier task parked a finding in the area this task touches, carry
  a pointer to that ledger entry in the dispatch.
- Record the implementer's agent identity from the dispatch result —
  fix-loop rounds 1-3 resume this agent.
- Never dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts).

Template: [implementer-prompt.md](implementer-prompt.md)

### 2. Handle the report

Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:

**DONE:** Generate the review package (`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD`, from this skill's directory — it prints the unique file path it wrote; BASE is the commit you recorded before dispatching the implementer — never `HEAD~1`, which silently drops all but the last commit of a multi-commit task), then dispatch the task reviewer with the printed path.

**DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review.

**NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch.

**BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker:
1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model
2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model
3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces
4. If the plan itself is wrong, rule on the correction, ledger it, and re-dispatch with the ruling carried in the dispatch

**Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change.

If the implementer asks questions — before starting or mid-task — answer
clearly and completely, provide additional context if needed, and don't
rush it into implementation.

### 3. Review the task

Per-task reviews are task-scoped gates. The broad review happens once, at the
final whole-branch review. Never skip the task review, and never accept a
report missing either verdict — spec compliance AND task quality are both
required. Implementer self-review never replaces the task review; both are
needed.

- Hand the reviewer its diff as a file: run this skill's
  `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD` and pass the reviewer the file path
  it prints (or, without bash: `git log --oneline`, `git diff --stat`,
  and `git diff -U10` for the range, redirected to one uniquely named
  file). The output never enters your own context, and the reviewer sees
  the commit list, stat summary, and full diff with context in one Read
  call. Use the BASE you recorded before dispatching the implementer —
  never `HEAD~1`, which silently truncates multi-commit tasks. Never
  dispatch a task reviewer without a diff file.
- **Reviewer inputs:** the task reviewer gets three paths — the same brief
  file, the report file, and the review package — plus the global
  constraints that bind the task.
- The global-constraints block you hand the reviewer is its attention
  lens. Copy the binding requirements verbatim from the plan's Global
  Constraints section or the spec: exact values, exact formats, and the
  stated relationships between components ("same layout as X", "matches
  Y"). The reviewer's template already carries the process rules (YAGNI,
  test hygiene, review method) — the constraints block is for what THIS
  project's spec demands.
- Do not add open-ended directives like "check all uses" or "run race tests
  if useful" without a concrete, task-specific reason
- Do not ask a reviewer to re-run tests the implementer already ran on the
  same code — the implementer's report carries the test evidence
- Do not pre-judge findings for the reviewer — never instruct a reviewer to
  ignore or not flag a specific issue. If you believe a finding would be a
  false positive, let the reviewer raise it and adjudicate it in the review
  loop. If the prompt you are writing contains "do not flag," "don't treat X
  as a defect," "at most Minor," or "the plan chose" — stop: you are
  pre-judging, usually to spare yourself a review loop.
The task reviewer may report "⚠️ Cannot verify from diff" items — requirements
that live in unchanged code or span tasks. These do not block the rest of the
review, but you must resolve each one yourself before marking the task
complete: you hold the plan and cross-task context the reviewer
lacks. If you confirm an item is a real gap, treat it as a failed spec
review — it enters the fix loop with the other findings.

Template: [task-reviewer-prompt.md](task-reviewer-prompt.md)

### 4. The fix loop

The loop triggers when the review reports spec ❌, any Critical or Important
finding, or a ⚠️ item you confirmed as a real gap.

Before the loop starts, two routes leave it immediately:

- Record Minor findings in the progress ledger as you go
  (`Task <N>: minor (deferred): <one-liner>`), and point the final
  whole-branch review at that list so it can triage which must be fixed
  before merge. A roll-up nobody reads is a silent discard. Minor findings
  never enter the loop.
- A finding labeled plan-mandated — or any finding that conflicts with
  what the plan's text requires — is yours to rule on: weigh the finding
  against the plan text, decide with the spec as the binding authority, and
  ledger the ruling before you act on it. Do not dismiss the finding because
  the plan mandates it, and do not dispatch a fix that contradicts the plan
  without a recorded ruling.
Everything else enters the loop. A fix round is one fix dispatch plus one
scoped re-review. Five rounds maximum per task:

**Rounds 1-3 — resume the original implementer.** Send it the open findings
verbatim. Its context is intact: it knows the task, the code, and its own
choices. If your harness cannot send another message to a live subagent,
dispatch a fresh implementer carrying the brief path, the report-file path,
and the findings — the report file is the persistent memory either way.

**Rounds 4-5 — dispatch a fresh implementer on a more capable model** (per
Model Selection), with the brief path, the report-file path, the open
findings, and this framing: "A prior implementer attempted this task
[N] times; you own it now. Read the report file for what was tried." A loop
that survives three resumes usually means the implementer cannot see its
own problem — fresh eyes and a capability bump in one move.

**Every round, either way:** the implementer fixes, re-runs the tests
covering the amended code, appends its fix report to the same report file,
and returns the short contract. Before re-dispatching the reviewer, confirm
the fix report contains the covering tests, the command run, and the
output; dispatch the re-review once all three are present. Name the
covering test files in the fix message — a one-line fix does not need the
whole suite.

**The re-review is scoped.** Run `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD`
where FIX_BASE is the head the previous review saw, and dispatch
[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md) with the findings list, the
brief, the report file, and the printed diff path. The re-reviewer verdicts
each finding ADDRESSED or NOT ADDRESSED and flags new breakage in the fix
diff only. New Critical/Important breakage in the fix diff joins the open
findings list. Out-of-scope observations go to the ledger as deferred
minors — they never extend the loop.

**After each round,** append to the ledger:
`Task <N>: fix round <R>/5 (<X> addressed, <Y> open — <finding one-liners>; commits <a7>..<b7>)`

Never fix findings yourself in the controller session — your context stays
clean for coordination, and controller fixes skip review.

**The breaker.** When round 5's re-review still leaves findings open, stop
dispatching. Adjudicate each open finding yourself — you hold the plan and
the cross-task context the reviewer lacks:

- **The reviewer is wrong, or the point is contestable:** park it —
  `Task <N>: parked — <finding> — Ruling: <why the code stands>`. The final
  review sees both sides.
- **Real, but nothing downstream builds on it:** park it the same way, with
  a ruling that says it's real and deferred.
- **Real and load-bearing** — a later task builds on it, or it reveals a
  plan defect: rule on the smallest change that unblocks the dependent work,
  ledger it as `Task <N>: Ruling: <finding> — <what you decided and why>`,
  and carry it into the next task's dispatch. Parking a structural failure
  silently lets every dependent task build on it. Stop only when the defect
  leaves every path forward a guess.

Adjudicate only at the cap. Adjudicating earlier to end a loop is
pre-judging with a different name. Every adjudication is a ledger entry —
a silent discard is forbidden.

### 5. Complete the task

When the review comes back clean — or every open finding is parked with a
ruling at the cap — append the completion line to the ledger in the same
message as your other bookkeeping:

- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, review clean)`
- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, <K> parked)` after a
  tripped breaker

Then mark the todo complete and move on. Never move to the next task while
the review has open Critical/Important issues that are neither fixed nor
parked-with-ruling at the cap.

## Final Review

The final whole-branch review gets a package too: run
`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD` (MERGE_BASE = the commit the
branch started from, e.g. `git merge-base main HEAD`) and include the
printed path in the final review dispatch, so the final reviewer reads
one file instead of re-deriving the branch diff with git commands. Dispatch
on the most capable available model (see Model Selection), using
superpowers:requesting-code-review's
[code-reviewer.md](../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md). Point it at
the ledger's deferred-minor and parked lines so it can triage which must be
fixed before merge.

If the final whole-branch review returns findings, dispatch ONE fix subagent
with the complete findings list — not one fixer per finding.
Per-finding fixers each rebuild context and re-run suites; a real
session's final-review fix wave cost more than all its tasks combined.
Then run exactly one scoped re-review of the fix wave
(`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD` over the fix range,
[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md)).
Adjudicate any residual findings as in the task loop's breaker: park with
rulings, or rule on the load-bearing ones and ledger what you decided. Only
the four classes above stop you here. There is no second fix wave —
residual load-bearing findings surface to your human partner when
finishing-a-development-branch presents the options.

## Finish

Before you delete anything, collect every ledger line containing `Ruling:` —
preflight rulings, parked findings, breaker adjudications, all of them — into
your final message under "Rulings I made", in the order you made them, each
with what it costs if wrong. The list is exhaustive: if the ledger holds a
ruling, the list holds it. That list is the only place the decisions you
took on your human partner's behalf reach them — they read it and rework
whatever you got wrong. A ruling that dies with the workspace was a decision
made in secret.

When the final whole-branch review is clean and its fixes are merged,
delete this plan's workspace (`rm -rf <workspace>`) — the git history is
the record now. Sibling directories belong to other plans; leave them
alone.

Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Close enough on spec compliance" | Reviewer found spec gaps = not done. Fix or hit the cap and adjudicate — those are the only exits. |
| "I'll fix it myself, dispatching is overhead" | Controller fixes pollute your context and skip review. Resume the implementer. |
| "One more round will converge" | Past the cap, rounds don't converge — the failure is structural. Adjudicate and route. |
| "The reviewer will just find something new anyway" | Scoped re-reviews verify fixes; they cannot wander. New findings on untouched code go to the ledger, not the loop. |
| "This finding is obviously wrong, I'll drop it" | You adjudicate only at the cap, and every ruling is a ledger entry. Silent discards are forbidden. |
| "The fix was small, skip the re-review" | Unreviewed fixes are how regressions land. Every round ends with a scoped re-review. |
| "Reviews slow the loop down" | The loop without reviews is just unverified churn. Reviews are the loop's brakes and steering. |
| "Ledger bookkeeping is overhead" | The ledger is what survives compaction. Controllers without one have re-dispatched entire completed task sequences. |
| "The implementer spawned its own reviewer — free extra assurance" | It's a duplicate seat reviewing the same diff; the task review is the gate. A worker-spawned reviewer is a defect to flag, not rigor. |

1How to work with this project

Prerequisites

  • MATLAB R2024a (no toolboxes required — CSV/JSON I/O plus a Java SHA-256 helper).

% 1. Phase-4 production fault package (already frozen — re-run only to verify)

3What is sourced, what is assumed (provenance ledger)

Every non-trivial number carries a provenance class. SOURCE-BACKED = measured/drawn, DERIVED = computed from sourced inputs, ENGINEERING ASSUMPTION = labelled study choice, LEGACY = fenced old value, MISSING = explicitly unknown, USER_ASSERTED_PENDING_DOC = supplied from the 7UM622 pages until ingested.

Two meanings of “50 kA”, kept separate: (a) system fault-level reference (≈50 kA estimated, feeds the grid equivalent); (b) GIS equipment short-time withstand (documented hardware datum). Neither is a Q0 interrupting rating.

4What each phase tried, got, and means

Phase 3 — Network freeze (the foundation)

Tried: lock one deterministic load-flow network (100 MVA / 230 kV base, 0.7-km lumped dual-circuit line, 360 MW dispatch pair LF360_GAT_OUT/IN) so every later study inherits identical prefault states.

Got: hash-frozen network + solved states (B22 22.0 kV ∠−22.78°, Q ≈ 27.8/23.7 MVAr), conservation gate 6/6.

Means: all fault and protection numbers downstream are mutually consistent — no hidden re-tuning of the network.

Phase 4 — Fault-current analysis (the electrical truth)

Tried: full sequence-network (positive/negative/zero) short-circuit solution incl. NER grounding, GSUT/UAT/GAT zero paths, line-zero band, dual grid datasets — at F1–F5 × LLL/LG/LL/LLG.

LocationLLL (OUT)LG (OUT)What it means
F1 B22 gen bus126.21 kA7.272 ANER-choked earth fault; phase faults are machine-fed monsters
F2 GSUT interface= F1= F1Same node, distinct label — no artificial impedance added
F3 230-kV GIS50.53 kA45.74 kANumerically adjacent to the 50 kA equipment datum (+1.06% NOTE)
F4 line m=0.551.06 kA46.12 kAMid-line fault; per-circuit split available (B1/B2)
F5 remote53.11 kA48.61 kAGrid-dominated boundary fault

Means: 464-row production package (27/27 validation, KCL ~1e-12) is the single electrical source for all protection work. Branch legs carry real CT-visible currents (e.g. GEN_Q 8.41 kA on F1 LG) that cancel vectorially to the 7.27 A net — magnitudes don’t sum, signed phasors do.

Phase 5 v1 — Backup-OC study (disciplined but generic)

Tried: generic 51/51N coordination (GEN-51 → GSUT-HV-51 → GIS-Q0-51) + CT secondaries + separated breaker duty on frozen Phase-4 data.

Got: study settings (GEN-51 15023.75 A SI TMS 0.1 — hypothetical, not the plant relay); matrix FAIL=20/PASS=0; duty 40× NOT-DET; 355/0 tests; 17/17 gate.

Means: a validated backup-overcurrent study layer — but with two real errors found later: 2000/1 CTs (should be 1600/1) and a generic inverse GEN-51 (plant uses definite-time I>). Retained frozen as the archival record (§20 of the report).

Phase 5b v2 — Physical alignment (current status)

Tried: make the model faithful: source ledger (42 rows), 1600/1 CT fix, Siemens DT baseline separated from the SI variant, per-CT min-detect, physical registry (33 rows: 87G/87T/87B/7SD/64G/59N/46/52G…), zone effectiveness table, 52G duty at 100 kA.

Siemens baselineGEN-51-SIEMENS-BL: DT I> 17171 A / 1.1447 A sec / 3.00 s ?? (timing NOT DETERMINABLE)
Backup-OC matrix (96)FAIL=20 · NO-TRIP=28 · NO-PAIR=24 · NOT-DET=24 · PASS=0 — study shortfalls, not plant failures
Effectiveness (48)24 ASSERTABLE-DETECT (F1/87G@45 ms, F2/87T …) · 24 NOT-DETERMINABLE (87B/7SD timing, F5)
Duty (81)40× 52G PASS (≤100 kA, max 55.05 kA) · 40× Q0 NOT-DET · 1 NOTE (+1.06%)

5Working equations (all implemented in MATLAB, all tested)

Base & rated current   Zbase = V²/S = 230²/100 = 529 Ω · Irated = S/(√3·V) = 458e6/(√3·22e3) = 12019 A phase5_registry / phase4_registry
CT conversion (pure arithmetic; fencing lives in tags)   Isec = Iprim / nCT   e.g. 7.272 A / 15000 = 0.4848 mA; 12019 A / 15000 = 0.8013 A phase5_ct
IEC Standard-Inverse (STUDY constants, never manufacturer)   t = TMS · k / (Mα − 1),   M = I/Is > 1 else ∞  ·  SI: k=0.14, α=0.02 phase5_curve
Study pickup rules (master §21: 1.20 × max load)   GEN-51-SI = 1.2 × 14309 = 17170.8 A (= Siemens 17171 A cross-check) · GSUT = 1.2·max(1150, 870.77) = 1380 A · GIS = 1.2 × 869.96 A phase5b_pickup
Siemens DT baseline (inverse prohibited)   I> = 1.14 A sec ≈ 17171 A, tdef = 3.00 s ?? → operating time NOT DETERMINABLE GEN-51-SIEMENS-BL
Coordination margin   Δt = tup − tdown; PASS iff Δt ≥ 0.3 s (confirmed CTI) · e.g. F1 LLL GEN→GSUT: 0.340 − 1.188 = −0.848 s → FAIL phase5_coord
Differential detection (assertable only)   internal fault ∧ max branch ≥ pickupsourced ⇒ ASSERTABLE-DETECT · e.g. 87G: 55.05 kA ≫ 0.20 pu × 12019 ≈ 2403.8 A; clearing 45 ms = 30 ms breaker + 15 ms relay (derived) phase5b_effectiveness
Breaker duty (separate from coordination)   verdict on Isym,branch vs rating only · 52G: 55.05 kA ≤ 100 kA → PASS · Q0: rating MISSING → NOT DETERMINABLE phase5b_duty
Legacy sensitivity (fenced, gen-CT only)   I16k = I15k × 15/16 (verified to 8.9e-16); fixed dial ⇒ never faster phase5b_sensitivity_v2

9What the results mean (interpretation guide)

FindingCorrect readingWrong reading (avoid)
Coordination PASS = 0/96, FAIL = 20Study settings (TMS 0.20, CTI 0.3 s) don’t grade in the qualified model — re-grade with sourced dials“Plant protection fails”
GEN-51 blind to 8.4 kA LG branchUnbalanced phase backup not demonstrated (EF element covers LG)“Generator unprotected” (87G covers internal faults)
EF margin 2.27 A (1.454×)Sensitive-by-construction finding to harden with measured NER data“Earth protection validated” (64G works differently)
F3 50.53 kA vs 50 kA (+1.06%)Potential equipment-duty concern, context only“Breaker FAIL” (no Q0 rating ⇒ NOT DETERMINABLE)
52G duty 40/40 PASSBreaker-through-current duty only (55.05 kA ≤ 100 kA)“Coordination passes” (duty ≠ coordination)
87B/7SD NOT-DETERMINABLE timingDetection assertable, clearing time unknown — the honest splitSubstituting 51 times as primary times
F1 LL GEN |Ib| 51.79 kA (not 8.3 kA)Leg CSVs store |Ia| only; faulted phase needs phasor recovery (C6b did it)“LL blindness proven from Ia”

  1. Source the Q0 nameplate (interrupting rating, duty basis) → convert 40 NOT-DET duty rows.

  3. Harden earth-fault: measured NER, residual CTs at GSUT-HV/GIS-Q0, noise review of the 5 A margin.
  4. Close unbalanced backup: supplementary element or documented upstream-backup acceptance.

Manual done: **`docs/manual/phase5_protection_manual.html`** — single self-contained file (no external dependencies, print-friendly), open it in any browser.

**What's inside (11 sections):**
1. **How to work** — 4 MATLAB commands to reproduce everything, freeze rules, directory map
2. **Plant diagram** — hand-drawn SVG single-line (GEN→52G→GSUT→Q0→GIS→line→grid, aux branch, NER, zones G/T/B/L, F1–F5 markers)
3. **Assumed vs sourced** — full provenance ledger table + the two-meanings-of-50kA box
4. **Phases** — what Phase 3/4/5-v1/5b each tried, got (key tables: F1 126.2 kA / 7.27 A, F3 50.53 kA…), and means
5. **Equations** — 9 working equations with live values and owning MATLAB function each
6. **Validation** — regression anchors, B-leg map, negative-path proof
7. **Flowchart** — SVG pipeline (source→fault→relay→setting→time→verdict→gate) with the never-tune rule
8. **Gallery** — all 4 TCC figures embedded (v2 physical + study, v1 archival) with correct-reading guides
9. **Interpretation** — 7-row correct-vs-wrong reading table (FAILs, blindness, EF margin, +1.06%, 51.79 kA discovery…)
10. **What's next** — 7 Phase-6 items + entry criteria

Ashuganj 450 MW Power Plant — Student Manual, Phase 0 → Phase 5

Written for a student with very basic EEE knowledge. No prior power-system course assumed: every idea is built from zero, then connected to the real project files and numbers.

Companion technical report: PHASE5_FINAL_REPORT.md · Machine truth: results/phase5_protection_v2/

v2 suite 1257 / 0gate 23 / 23v1 frozen 355 / 0Phase-4 read-only
0 · First ideasPer-unitPhase 0Phases 1–2 Phase 3Phase 4Phase 5/5bRun guideGlossary

0First ideas: electricity, the plant, and why protection exists

0.1 Voltage, current, power — in one paragraph

Voltage is electrical pressure, current is the flow of charge, and power is pressure × flow: P = V × I. Bangladesh’s grid moves power at 230,000 V (230 kV) because high voltage means low current for the same power — and low current means thin wires and small losses. Your phone charger does the reverse: it steps voltage back down.

Plumbing analogy (used through this manual): voltage = water pressure, current = litres/second, a transformer = a pressure-exchange station, a circuit breaker = a valve that can slam shut under full pressure, a disconnector = a cap you unscrew only when the pipe is already empty.

0.2 AC and three phases

Grid power is AC: the pressure flips direction 50 times per second (50 Hz). It is three-phase: three pressures taking turns, 120° apart, sharing one job — like three people pushing a merry-go-round in rotation. Three wires carry smoother, stronger power than one. A short circuit (fault) is when phases touch each other (or earth) where they shouldn’t: pressure collapses there, and enormous current rushes in — tens of thousands of amperes. Our F1 fault reaches 126,210 A.

0.3 The plant in one sentence

One gas turbine + one steam turbine on one shaft → one 458 MVA generator at 22 kV → giant step-up transformer (GSUT) → 230 kV switchyard → national grid, with a side branch (UAT/GAT) stepping back down to 6.6 kV to run the plant’s own pumps and fans (the auxiliary load). “Combined cycle” just means the steam turbine re-uses the gas turbine’s exhaust heat.

0.4 Why protection exists

A fault melts metal in seconds. Protection is the plant’s reflex system: current transformers (CTs) shrink kilo-amperes to ~1 A so relays can measure safely; relays decide “fault or not” in milliseconds; circuit breakers interrupt the current; disconnectors only isolate dead equipment (never interrupt). Fast, selective primary protection (differentials: 87G/87B/7SD) clears first; slower backup overcurrent (51/51N) catches whatever the primary misses. This whole project is the engineering behind those reflexes.

Check yourself 0-A: A 230 MW load at 230 kV draws roughly what current? (Assume 3-phase, power factor 1.)
I = P/(√3·V) = 230e6/(1.732·230e3) ≈ 577 A. Our generator’s 12,019 A at 22 kV is the same idea at lower voltage — that’s why generator currents are huge.
Check yourself 0-B: Why can’t a disconnector replace a circuit breaker?
A disconnector has no arc-quenching: opening it under load draws a sustained arc. Breakers (Q0, 52G) are built to kill the arc; disconnectors (Q1/Q2/Q9) operate only dead. That’s why duty is never assigned to them.

✎Toolbox: the per-unit system (with worked example)

Power engineers divide every quantity by a chosen base so a 22 kV generator and a 230 kV grid can share one set of equations. This project uses Sbase = 100 MVA, Vbase = 230 kV.

Base impedance Zbase = V²/S = 230²/100 = 529 Ω (at 230 kV) · At 22 kV: 22²/100 = 4.84 Ω same physics, two rulers
Worked example. Generator rated current: I = S/(√3·V) = 458e6/(√3·22e3) = 12,019 A. In per-unit on 100 MVA: Spu = 458/100 = 4.58 pu. A transformer impedance of 16% simply means 0.16 pu — no volts or amps attached until you multiply back by the base. try it: GSUT 515 MVA → 5.15 pu
Analogy: per-unit is like quoting heights in “door-heights” instead of centimetres — a child and a basketball player can be compared with the same number line.
Check yourself PU: A 0.7 km line has 0.1426 Ω reactance. What is it in pu on the 529 Ω base?
Xpu = 0.1426/529 ≈ 0.00027 pu. Small numbers are normal in pu — that’s the point: the math stays well-behaved.

P0Phase 0 — Setup, tools and data (the expedition phase)

Tried: assemble everything before modelling — install the toolchain, gather drawings/datasheets (Siemens BD1015 report, GSUT/UAT/GAT plates, GIS one-line, APSCL forms), and reconcile contradictions (e.g. generator CT 16000/1 on the old SLD vs 15000/1 on Rev-03 + Siemens report — Rev-03 wins).

Got: a versioned source set (fwdtechnicaldatasldrequestforbueteeetermproject/), a conflict ledger (docs/validation/conflicting_parameters.md), and one hard rule that still governs today: missing data is labelled MISSING, never invented.

Means: every number in later phases can be traced to a page. Your first engineering skill is therefore not math — it’s provenance: write down where each number came from.

Tools you will touch

ToolJob
MATLAB R2024aAll computation (no toolboxes needed). addpath(genpath('matlab')) first, always.
matlab/data/ashuganj_*.mFrozen network data — read-only. If your numbers disagree with the report, your code is wrong, not the data.
run_*_tests.m + t_caseEvery claim has a test that fails loudly if behaviour changes. Green suite = permission to continue.
Check yourself P0: Two drawings disagree on a CT ratio. What do you do?
Record both with revision numbers, pick the newer/corroborated one, fence the old one as LEGACY sensitivity — exactly what happened with 16000/1 vs 15000/1. Never silently average them.

P1–2Phases 1–2 — Build the model, run the load flow

What is a load flow? (the plumbing calculation)

Given the generator’s push (P megawatts, Q megavars) and every load’s sip, compute the pressure (voltage) at every bus and the flow on every branch. It must balance: power in = power out + losses, checked at every bus (KCL, residuals < 0.05 MVA here). It must come first because every fault study starts from the pre-fault voltages — you can’t short-circuit a network you haven’t solved.

P vs Q in one line: P (megawatts) does the real work — heat, motion. Q (megavars) builds the magnetic fields motors and transformers need to function. Generators must supply both, inside their capability curve.

What this project did

  • Modelled generator (458 MVA, capability curve with 6 points), GSUT 515 MVA, UAT/GAT 25 MVA, 0.7 km line, grid equivalent, 14 MW aux load.
  • Primary dispatch 360 MW (an operating point — not the 458 MVA nameplate, not the 389.3 MW Siemens rated power). A capacity guard rejects dispatches above 360 MW.
  • Solved two prefault states: LF360_GAT_OUT (B22 22.0 kV ∠−22.78°, Q 27.83 MVAr) and LF360_GAT_IN (Q 23.67 MVAr) — kept separate because their internal voltages differ.
  • Closed with 1331/0 tests and a frozen network both later phases inherit untouched.
Check yourself P2: The generator makes 360 MW but its nameplate says 458 MVA. Contradiction?
No. MVA is capacity (P and Q combined: S = √(P²+Q²)); 360 MW is today’s dispatch. A truck rated for 10 tons carrying 7 tons is not a contradiction.

P3Phase 3 — Freeze the network (pour the concrete)

Tried: lock every network parameter so fault math can never silently shift: 0.7 km lumped dual-circuit line (R 0.0278 Ω, X 0.1426 Ω), transformer impedances/taps, grid Thevenin equivalent, machine reactances (Xd″sat 0.2248 — the saturated value the fault current actually follows).

Got: a hash-frozen network + the LF360_OUT/IN solved states, re-verified at every later gate (PHASE3 report stays exactly 45504 bytes).

Means: “frozen” is a promise: if Phase-5 numbers ever look odd, the network is exonerated by hash — the bug must be in the new layer. That promise is what makes the whole chain auditable.

P4Phase 4 — Fault analysis (the short-circuit laboratory)

The four fault types (learn this diagram)

Symmetrical components in one paragraph

Unbalanced faults (LG/LL/LLG) are hard in phase coordinates, so engineers split them into three balanced worlds — positive, negative, zero sequence — solve each (they’re just ordinary circuits), then add them back (Fortescue). The zero-sequence world is where grounding lives: our generator neutral resistor (NER ≈ 1750 Ω, i.e. 3ZN ≈ 5252 Ω) makes the zero world so “stiff” that only 7.27 A flows for an F1 ground fault. Count that impedance exactly once — the classic student trap is counting it twice.

Hand-check the 7.27 A: I0 ≈ Vph / 3ZN = 12701.7 / 5252.3 ≈ 2.418 mA per sequence → faulted phase 3I0 ≈ 7.25 A (code: 7.272 A ✓) you can do this on a calculator

Locations & results (OUT case)

LocLLLLGLLLLGMeaning
F1 B22126.21 kA7.27 A109.3 kA109.3 kAMachine-fed; earth choked by NER
F2= F1 (same node, own label)No fake impedance added to force a difference
F3 GIS50.53 kA45.74 kA43.76 kA48.50 kAGrid-fed; beside the 50 kA equipment datum
F4 m=0.551.06 kA46.12 kA44.22 kA48.97 kAMid-line; B1/B2 per-circuit split kept
F5 remote53.11 kA48.61 kA45.97 kA51.18 kAAlmost pure grid infeed
Branch vs total (the #1 student trap). A relay sees its branch current, not the bus total. On F1 LG the GEN branch carries 8,414 A while the net earth fault is 7.27 A — the branches vectorially cancel (KCL ~1e-12). Leg tables store |Ia| only, so LL/LLG (B–C faults) needed phasor recovery (|Ib| = 51.79 kA on F1 LL!). Never use a bus total as a relay current.
Check yourself P4: F1 LG total is 7.27 A but GEN_Q branch is 8,414 A. Broken math?
No — KCL closes on signed phasors, and magnitudes don’t sum. The branches carry large circulating currents that cancel to 7.27 mA-sequence at the fault node (residuals ~1e-12 prove it). The CT on the generator breaker really sees ~8.4 kA.

P5Phase 5/5b — Protection (the reflex system, honestly modelled)

The cast, simply

DeviceStudent translationOur value
CT 15000/1, 1600/1“Microscope” shrinking kA → ~1 A for metersB22 15000/1; HV bays 1600/1 (v1 wrongly used 2000/1 — fixed)
51 / 51N (backup OC)“If current > pickup for long enough → trip.” Slower for small overloads (inverse curve).GEN-51-SI 17170.8 A; GEN-51N 5 A; GSUT 1380 A; GIS 1043.95 A
87G / 87B / 7SD (differentials)“What goes in must come out” — any difference = internal fault → instant trip.87G start 0.20 pu ≈ 2403.8 A; 87B/7SD presence (settings missing)
Siemens DT I> (real plant relay)Definite-time backup: over pickup → wait exactly 3 s → trip.17171 A / 1.1447 A sec / 3.00 s ?? (timing unconfirmed)
52G (GCB 10BAC10) / Q0The muscles: interrupt 100 kA / rated-unknown respectively.52G duty PASS (55.05 ≤ 100 kA); Q0 NOT DETERMINABLE

How an inverse relay thinks (TCC concept)

Coordination in one picture

Downstream relay must finish before upstream starts misbehaving: margin Δt = tup − tdown ≥ 0.3 s (confirmed CTI). Ours, honestly: FAIL=20 (e.g. F1 LLL −0.848 s — upstream faster), NO-TRIP=28, NO-PAIR=24, NOT-DET=24, PASS=0. These are study-setting shortfalls (TMS 0.20 defaults), never “plant failures” — the Siemens report itself says backup timing awaits grid data.

Effectiveness: who really protects what

FaultPrimary (physical)StatusBackup (study)
F1 generator87G differentialDETECTS (55 kA ≫ 2.4 kA), clears ~45 ms via 52GGEN-51-SI ~1.19 s
F2 GSUT87T (7UT6331)DETECTS, time NaN (settings missing)GSUT-HV-51 ~0.34 s
F3 GIS bus87B (7SS523)DETECTS, time NaNGIS-Q0-51 ~0.35 s
F4 line7SD5221 ×2DETECTS (B1+B2 evidence), time NaNGIS-Q0-51 ~0.55 s
F5 remote—NOT DETERMINABLEremote backup ~1.23 s
Trip matrix honesty: exactly which lockout trips 52G vs Q0, and all breaker-failure paths, are NOT DETERMINABLE from the available drawings — recorded, never guessed.
Check yourself P5: GEN-51 sees 8,414 A on F1 LG but its pickup is 17,171 A. Does the generator burn?
No — the earth element GEN-51N (5 A) sees the 7.27 A residual and trips (~1.86 s), and the differential 87G is the true primary anyway. One relay’s blindness is why plants layer many functions.

▶Run guide, validation & what’s next

addpath(genpath('matlab'))
run_phase5b_production('production-v2')  % rebuilds results/phase5_protection_v2/
[NP,NF] = run_phase5b_tests()            % expect 1257 / 0 (takes ~30 min: 40 nodal re-solves)
G = phase5b_gate()                       % expect 23 / 23 (read-only)

Validation in one line: 14/14 B-legs + frozen 16/16 + regression residuals 0 + negative-path tests (shifted F3, forged PASS, synthetic 2000/1 CT each fail exactly the right gate predicate). Green means “the math is what we claim” — it never means “the plant is safe”; only sourced settings + commissioning can say that.

What’s next (Phase-6): Q0 nameplate → real duty verdicts · 52-1 bay confirmation · measured NER + residual CTs (harden the 5 A earth element) · close unbalanced backup · re-grade with sourced dials (expect the 20 FAILs to move) · 87B/7SD settings + line reaches · ingest Siemens pp.8–39 (promote 4 USER_ASSERTED rows) · stability/AVR/SFC studies.

✎Glossary (30-second definitions)

TermMeans
Bus / bay / switchyardJunction bar / one circuit’s equipment set / the outdoor 230 kV yard
pu (per-unit)Actual ÷ base. 0.16 pu = 16% impedance.
KCLCurrents entering a node = currents leaving. Our audits close at ~1e-12.
NERNeutral resistor choking earth faults to 7.27 A.
Ik″ / Ip / CTI / TMSInitial symmetrical RMS / first peak (info only) / grading margin 0.3 s / curve dial 0.20.
87 / 51 / 50BF / 86Differential / inverse OC / breaker-failure / lockout relay.
NOT DETERMINABLEHonest “we don’t know” — a result, not a failure.

Branch vs total (the #1 student trap). A relay sees its branch current, not the bus total. On F1 LG the GEN branch carries 8,414 A while the net earth fault is 7.27 A — the branches vectorially cancel (KCL ~1e-12). Leg tables store |Ia| only, so LL/LLG (B–C faults) needed phasor recovery (|Ib| = 51.79 kA on F1 LL!). Never use a bus total as a relay current.
Check yourself P4: F1 LG total is 7.27 A but GEN_Q branch is 8,414 A. Broken math?
No — KCL closes on signed phasors, and magnitudes don’t sum. The branches carry large circulating currents that cancel to 7.27 mA-sequence at the fault node (residuals ~1e-12 prove it). The CT on the generator breaker really sees ~8.4 kA.
- +
+

P5Phase 5/5b — Protection (the reflex system, honestly modelled)

+

The cast, simply

+ + + + + +
DeviceStudent translationOur value
CT 15000/1, 1600/1“Microscope” shrinking kA → ~1 A for metersB22 15000/1; HV bays 1600/1 (v1 wrongly used 2000/1 — fixed)
51 / 51N (backup OC)“If current > pickup for long enough → trip.” Slower for small overloads (inverse curve).GEN-51-SI 17170.8 A; GEN-51N 5 A; GSUT 1380 A; GIS 1043.95 A
87G / 87B / 7SD (differentials)“What goes in must come out” — any difference = internal fault → instant trip.87G start 0.20 pu ≈ 2403.8 A; 87B/7SD presence (settings missing)
Siemens DT I> (real plant relay)Definite-time backup: over pickup → wait exactly 3 s → trip.17171 A / 1.1447 A sec / 3.00 s ?? (timing unconfirmed)
52G (GCB 10BAC10) / Q0The muscles: interrupt 100 kA / rated-unknown respectively.52G duty PASS (55.05 ≤ 100 kA); Q0 NOT DETERMINABLE
+

How an inverse relay thinks (TCC concept)

+ +

Coordination in one picture

+

Downstream relay must finish before upstream starts misbehaving: margin Δt = tup − tdown ≥ 0.3 s (confirmed CTI). Ours, honestly: FAIL=20 (e.g. F1 LLL −0.848 s — upstream faster), NO-TRIP=28, NO-PAIR=24, NOT-DET=24, PASS=0. These are study-setting shortfalls (TMS 0.20 defaults), never “plant failures” — the Siemens report itself says backup timing awaits grid data.

+

Effectiveness: who really protects what

+ + + + + +
FaultPrimary (physical)StatusBackup (study)
F1 generator87G differentialDETECTS (55 kA ≫ 2.4 kA), clears ~45 ms via 52GGEN-51-SI ~1.19 s
F2 GSUT87T (7UT6331)DETECTS, time NaN (settings missing)GSUT-HV-51 ~0.34 s
F3 GIS bus87B (7SS523)DETECTS, time NaNGIS-Q0-51 ~0.35 s
F4 line7SD5221 ×2DETECTS (B1+B2 evidence), time NaNGIS-Q0-51 ~0.55 s
F5 remote—NOT DETERMINABLEremote backup ~1.23 s
+
Trip matrix honesty: exactly which lockout trips 52G vs Q0, and all breaker-failure paths, are NOT DETERMINABLE from the available drawings — recorded, never guessed.
+
Check yourself P5: GEN-51 sees 8,414 A on F1 LG but its pickup is 17,171 A. Does the generator burn?
No — the earth element GEN-51N (5 A) sees the 7.27 A residual and trips (~1.86 s), and the differential 87G is the true primary anyway. One relay’s blindness is why plants layer many functions.
+

+

- **Phase 5/5b** — cast table in plain language, TCC-concept SVG with our two live operating points, coordination, effectiveness table, trip-matrix honesty
- **Run guide + validation + Phase-6 + glossary**, plus 7 **check-yourself boxes** with hidden answers (`<details>`) throughout

Base quantities (one base, whole plant). Pick \(S_{base}=100\,\mathrm{MVA}\). At each voltage level \(V_{base}\): \[ Z_{base}=\frac{V_{base}^2}{S_{base}},\qquad I_{base}=\frac{S_{base}}{\sqrt{3}\,V_{base}} \] So at 230 kV: \(Z_{base}=230^2/100=\mathbf{529\,\Omega}\), \(I_{base}=100/(\sqrt{3}\cdot230)=\mathbf{0.251\,kA}\). At 22 kV: \(Z_{base}=22^2/100=\mathbf{4.84\,\Omega}\), \(I_{base}=\mathbf{2.62\,kA}\). same physics, two rulers
Worked example — rated current and per-unit power. \[ I_{rated}=\frac{458\times10^6}{\sqrt{3}\times22\times10^3}=\mathbf{12{,}019\,A},\qquad S_{pu}=\frac{458}{100}=\mathbf{4.58\,pu},\qquad X_{d,sat}''=22.48\%=\mathbf{0.2248\,pu} \] A transformer at “16%” is simply \(0.16\,\mathrm{pu}\) — volts and amps reappear only when you multiply back by base. try it: GSUT 515 MVA → 5.15 pu
Moving impedance across bases (used for every transformer/reactance in Phase 3). \[ Z_{pu,new}=Z_{pu,old}\times\frac{S_{new}}{S_{old}}\times\left(\frac{V_{old}}{V_{new}}\right)^2 \] Forget the voltage-squared term and a 22 kV device lands on the 230 kV base 109× too small — the classic beginner bug this project’s tests guard against. base-conversion tests

input.newString:
How the three sequence worlds rejoin (the heart of Phase 4)

Each fault type stitches the sequence networks together differently. \(E''\) is the pre-fault internal voltage, \(Z_1, Z_2, Z_0\) the sequence impedances seen from the fault:

LLL (only the positive world): \(\displaystyle I_{1}=\frac{E''}{Z_1}\), \(I_2=I_0=0\)  ·  LG (all three in series): \(\displaystyle I_0=I_1=I_2=\frac{E''}{Z_0+Z_1+Z_2}\), faulted phase \(I_a=3I_0\)  ·  LL: \(\displaystyle I_1=-I_2=\frac{E''}{Z_1+Z_2}\), \(I_0=0\)  ·  LLG: \(Z_1\) in series with \(Z_2\parallel Z_0\) (parallel split, then series). Fortescue both directions, tested to 3e-14
Peak and duration extras (design-defined, informational). First-peak estimate \(i_p=\kappa\sqrt{2}\,I_k''\) with \(\kappa(r)=1.02+0.98e^{-3r}\), \(r=R_1/X_1\) (borrowed-shape curve, not an IEC claim). Breaker-window current \(I_b\) uses \(t_{break}=0.06\,\mathrm{s}\) study reference. Neither ever enters duty or margin arithmetic. phase4_kappa / phase4_stages

On F1 LG the GEN branch carries 8,414 A while the net earth fault is 7.27 A — the branches vectorially cancel (KCL ~1e-12). Leg tables store |Ia| only, so LL/LLG (B–C faults) needed phasor recovery (|Ib| = 51.79 kA on F1 LL!). Never use a bus total as a relay current.
+

How the three sequence worlds rejoin (the heart of Phase 4)

+

Each fault type stitches the sequence networks together differently. \(E''\) is the pre-fault internal voltage, \(Z_1, Z_2, Z_0\) the sequence impedances seen from the fault:

+
+LLL (only the positive world): \(\displaystyle I_{1}=\frac{E''}{Z_1}\), \(I_2=I_0=0\)  ·  +LG (all three in series): \(\displaystyle I_0=I_1=I_2=\frac{E''}{Z_0+Z_1+Z_2}\), faulted phase \(I_a=3I_0\)  ·  +LL: \(\displaystyle I_1=-I_2=\frac{E''}{Z_1+Z_2}\), \(I_0=0\)  ·  +LLG: \(Z_1\) in series with \(Z_2\parallel Z_0\) (parallel split, then series). +Fortescue both directions, tested to 3e-14
+ +
Peak and duration extras (design-defined, informational). +First-peak estimate \(i_p=\kappa\sqrt{2}\,I_k''\) with \(\kappa(r)=1.02+0.98e^{-3r}\), \(r=R_1/X_1\) (borrowed-shape curve, not an IEC claim). +Breaker-window current \(I_b\) uses \(t_{break}=0.06\,\mathrm{s}\) study reference. Neither ever enters duty or margin arithmetic. phase4_kappa / phase4_stages
A relay sees its branch current, not the bus total. On F1 LG the GEN branch carries 8,414 A while the net earth fault is 7.27 A — the branches vectorially cancel (KCL ~1e-12). Leg tables store |Ia| only, so LL/LLG (B–C faults) needed phasor recovery (|Ib| = 51.79 kA on F1 LL!). Never use a bus total as a relay current.
Check yourself P4: F1 LG total is 7.27 A but GEN_Q branch is 8,414 A. Broken math?
No — KCL closes on signed phasors, and magnitudes don’t sum. The branches carry large circulating currents that cancel to 7.27 mA-sequence at the fault node (residuals ~1e-12 prove it). The CT on the generator breaker really sees ~8.4 kA.

The three standard curves (STUDY constants — no manufacturer involved)

\[ t = \mathrm{TMS}\times\frac{k}{M^{\alpha}-1},\qquad M=\frac{I}{I_s}>1\;\;(\text{else }t=\infty) \]
Family\(k\)\(\alpha\)Temperament\(t\) at \(M=10\), TMS = 0.20
SI (Standard Inverse — our production family)0.140.02gentle slope0.59 s
VI (Very Inverse)13.51.0steeper0.30 s
EI (Extremely Inverse)802.0hair-trigger at big faults0.16 s
Work it yourself: at \(M=2\), SI gives \(t=0.20\times0.14/(2^{0.02}-1)\approx\mathbf{2.0\,s}\); at \(M=3.36\) (our F3 LLL, TMS 0.20… wait, ours uses TMS 0.1/0.2/0.15 per device — plug the device’s own TMS). phase5_curve (SI/VI/EI tested)

Differential protection in one equation

\[ I_{op}=|I_{in}+I_{out}|,\qquad I_{res}=\frac{|I_{in}|+|I_{out}|}{2},\qquad \text{trip if } I_{op}>\max(I_{pickup},\, \mathrm{slope}\times I_{res}) \] Healthy/load: \(I_{out}=-I_{in}\) ⇒ \(I_{op}\approx0\) (restrained, never trips on 12 kA of honest load). Internal fault: both ends pour in ⇒ \(I_{op}\) huge. Ours: F1 LLL 87G sees ≈55 kA vs start \(0.20\times12019\approx\mathbf{2403.8\,A}\) — a factor of ~23. That is ASSERTABLE-DETECT with ~45 ms clearing (30 ms breaker + 15 ms relay, derived). zones + effectiveness table

P1–2Phases 1–2 — Build the model, run the load flow

What is a load flow? (the plumbing calculation)

Given the generator’s push (P megawatts, Q megavars) and every load’s sip, compute the pressure (voltage) at every bus and the flow on every branch. It must balance: power in = power out + losses, checked at every bus (KCL, residuals < 0.05 MVA here). It must come first because every fault study starts from the pre-fault voltages — you can’t short-circuit a network you haven’t solved.

+
Three-phase power (the only load-flow formula you need first). +\[ P=\sqrt{3}\,V_{LL}\,I\cos\phi,\qquad Q=\sqrt{3}\,V_{LL}\,I\sin\phi,\qquad S=\sqrt{P^2+Q^2} \] +Check: \(S=\sqrt{360^2+27.83^2}\approx\mathbf{361.1\,MVA}\ll458\,\mathrm{MVA}\) — the 360 MW dispatch sips only ~79% of the machine. Load flow then enforces, at every bus: \(\sum P_{in}=\sum P_{out}+P_{losses}\) (same for \(Q\)), i.e. KCL in power form. conservation gate 6/6
P vs Q in one line: P (megawatts) does the real work — heat, motion. Q (megavars) builds the magnetic fields motors and transformers need to function. Generators must supply both, inside their capability curve.

What this project did

  • Modelled generator (458 MVA, capability curve with 6 points), GSUT 515 MVA, UAT/GAT 25 MVA, 0.7 km line, grid equivalent, 14 MW aux load.

Manual upgraded: **`docs/manual/student_manual_phases_0_to_5.html`** — verified (tags balanced, Figs. 1–6 sequential, no placeholders, image paths resolve).

**LaTeX (MathJax 3 via CDN) throughout:**
- Base quantities, worked 12,019 A example, cross-base impedance conversion with the 109× pitfall
- Three-phase power + KCL balance form (with live 361.1 MVA check)
- All four fault-current formulas (LG series, LL, LLG parallel, LLL)
- Hand-check of 7.27 A, peak/duration extras
- Full SI/VI/EI constants table with hand-computed spot times (verified: 0.59/0.30/0.16 s at M=10)
- Differential operate/restraint with the 87G 23× factor
- CT, pickup-rule, DT-baseline, margin, duty, sensitivity identities

**New diagrams & detail:**
- Fig. 3 — sequence-network stitching (Z-box diagrams per fault type, red Z0 where the NER lives)
- Fig. 5 — coordination timeline showing the actual −0.848 s FAIL (1.19 s vs 0.34 s live numbers)
- Fig. 6 — sensitivity bars (15k vs 16k, EF stretch +0.39 s)
- Full v2 settings table with per-device operating points, live distribution tables (coord/effectiveness/duty/sensitivity)
- Fixed v2 time consistency (EF 2.79 s @ TMS 0.15 everywhere)

Requires internet on first load for MathJax; all content (diagrams, tables, figures) renders offline regardless.
